name: Nora Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. Could you describe an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and repair street power feeders and pole-top transformers for the electricity company. I earned my vocational certificate through an apprenticeship, and I know the older blocks well, though I'm a regular crew worker rather than a supervisor. I like seeing residents' windows light again; traffic and long waits for access wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner cooks at a school, and our children have grown up and moved out. My line pay is above the usual rate, we have about nine months of expenses saved and there are plenty of other utilities nearby. Retirement is in sight but we have not picked a date; I use AI now and then to tidy a fault report, checking it against my notebook afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a shorter job form is fine, but someone still has to find the hot transformer on the street. The neighbours care when the lights return, not which app made the order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and my partner's school kitchen hours feel steady. We have nine months of expenses saved, our grown children are independent, and I can keep thinking about retirement without rushing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay on the street feeder repair rota and check each transformer reading with the crew. When I occasionally use AI to tidy a fault report, I will still compare the address and part number with my notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our money and my work. I would welcome fewer forms at the end of a long shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did that street resident need from the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An older resident once brought us tea after we restored the block's power. The resident needed a working power transformer and a crew that came back to check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend differently if the hype faded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not spend savings just because AI did less than promised. We'll keep the monthly bills and our existing reserve, then decide our retirement date from actual income figures.

say: **Street transformers** still need crews to diagnose and repair them despite shorter forms.
Residents need **working power** and a follow-up check more than a polished report.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and two wages leave retirement timing open without pressure.
A little **form automation** does not threaten my hands-on linework.
do: **Keep** the street feeder repair rota and physical transformer readings.
**Check** occasional AI-tidied reports against notebook addresses and part numbers.
feel: **Calm** about wages and pleased to lose some paperwork.
S0.quote: The resident needed a working power transformer and a crew that came back to check it.
fieldNote: Her concern stays with **service to residents** even in a mild technology world.
She uses AI **occasionally** for text and verifies addresses against her notebook.

steps.text: Keep street feeder repairs and physical transformer readings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may book outages, answer calls and order parts before robots can fix a pole. A missed access note can leave a street without power longer, so crews need a way to correct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair wage looks fairly safe, but faster booking could squeeze a full day's calls into fewer paid hours. I want to see the roster before I decide whether the change helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare the approved AI outage plan with our last four street repairs, including who needed a return visit. If the tool holds up, I'll take paid training on correcting its call list, and I'll track my hours for six months after the new schedule starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible hours cut, though nine months saved and nearby utilities give me choices. I am interested in a proven tool, not a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if AI dropped a return visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would phone dispatch from the site and put the resident's address back on the list before leaving. A missed power restoration visit is not a statistic to a resident in a dark flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell whether paid hours actually fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare six months of pay slips with the same months last year and mark the paid callout hours. If they fall, I will take the figures to the supervisor and ask how the company plans to cover the lost pay.

say: **AI outage lists** need field corrections when a resident still lacks power.
**Office booking** may change sooner than physical transformer repairs.
think: A faster **call schedule** could reduce my paid hours even if my repair job stays.
Our **strong savings** give me time to compare wages and consider nearby crews.
do: **Test** AI outage plans against four completed street repairs.
**Take** paid call-list training if the four-job comparison succeeds.
**Track** six months of callout hours after any schedule change.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hour loss, while able to test the new system.
S1.quote: A missed power restoration visit is not a statistic to a resident in a dark flat.
fieldNote: Her mood follows the **possible paid-hour loss**, not mere discomfort with AI.
She wants **four-job evidence** and paid training before adopting a new call list.

steps.text: Test AI outage list against four completed street repairs
Take paid call-list training if four-job comparison succeeds
Track six months of paid callout hours after schedule changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI by 2028 can answer outage calls and plan routes before capable field robots arrive around 2031. Our electricity company should say which repair crews remain and who checks the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be about 63 at the robot date and may still want to work. My nine months of savings will not tell me whether I can afford to stop repairing power lines at 63. An early loss of shifts could change our retirement calculations, even if the school kitchen keeps paying my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask for the 2028 call-centre and 2031 field crew plans and compare our retirement income with current bills. If paid robot inspection training with actual controls opens, I'll enrol; if a formal cut comes first, I'll apply to a nearby utility crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real possibility of losing paid repair hours before we choose to leave. I have options, but none is an actual job offer today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown son we are checking options, not looking for him to carry us. He has his own household, and my wage is still coming in today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the inspection course worth enrolling in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A useful course would be paid by the company, include a real field robot and let me practise the stop control. I would not enrol in a screen-only class just to say I had retrained.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches calls and routing before field robots arrive around 2031.
The company should publish **repair crew plans** and name who checks robot work.
think: At about **63**, I may still rely on line shifts when robots enter the field.
Nine months of **savings** helps but does not settle a long wage gap.
do: **Ask** company for 2028 call-centre and 2031 repair crew plans.
**Compare** retirement income with bills before changing work plans.
**Enrol** in company-paid robot inspection training if real controls practice opens.
feel: **Anxious** about possible repair-hour loss, with savings and local options.
S2.quote: My nine months of savings will not tell me whether I can afford to stop repairing power lines at 63.
fieldNote: She is concerned with **retirement timing** and genuine repair-hour risk rather than certain loss.
Training is a **conditional enrolment** with company payment and hands-on controls.
A nearby job move requires a **formal cut**; none has occurred.

steps.text: Ask company for call-centre and repair crew plans
Compare retirement income with household bills
Enrol in company-paid robot inspection training if controls practice opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years allows the electricity company to test robots on a real street circuit before 2034, after thinking AI changes call planning in 2031. Residents and lineworkers should see the results, not just a launch video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 66 I might have stepped away from the repair rota if our retirement sums work. If I still need wages, a paid ground inspection job would be less tiring than climbing, but I cannot count on a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll join the local union safety meeting to ask for published robot trial faults and a named worker with stop authority. At home we'll review our retirement sums each year, and I'll apply for a paid ground inspector post only if it opens with wages that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the chance of still needing wages when field robots arrive. The longer runway lets us plan, but it does not guarantee an affordable exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a realistic robot trial have to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the trial team how it handles a blocked street and an older pole-top transformer. A clean robot display in a yard will not show who repairs a power transformer in traffic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a ground inspector post real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a regular roster, field duties and pay high enough for our household bills. A one-day visit to watch a robot would not become a ground inspector job.

say: **Real street trials** should publish faults before robots reach line repairs around 2034.
**Residents and workers** should see evidence after thinking AI changes call planning in 2031.
think: At about **66**, retirement may be affordable, but the figures are not settled.
A paid **ground inspector job** might help if I still need wages then.
do: **Join** a union safety meeting to request public trial faults and stop authority.
**Review** retirement sums with my partner each year.
**Apply** for paid ground inspector post if roster and wages cover bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible wage gap, despite more planning time.
S3.quote: A clean robot display in a yard will not show who repairs a power transformer in traffic.
fieldNote: She seeks **published faults** and stop authority through a local union meeting.
She treats a ground role as **conditional paid work**, with no vacancy promised.

steps.text: Join union safety meeting on trial faults and stop authority
Review retirement sums with partner annually
Apply for paid ground inspector post if roster and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 will change calls and planning first, and capable field robots around 2039 come when I will be about 71. I hope to have left regular repair shifts by then if our finances allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The decade makes me calmer about my own job, though I still want the next crews trained and residents told who fixes an outage. I will not pretend an exact retirement date is already decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year my partner and I will review our retirement statements and set the minimum monthly income we need. I'll keep the repair rota while it suits me, and I will take our union branch's safety notes to a younger worker before I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the long runway and grateful for the choice to hand over carefully. A power outage still needs a named worker when a resident calls, even if robots lift the transformer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown daughter about this trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown daughter the next lineworkers should learn both the meter and the machine stop control. She works elsewhere now, so I would offer an opinion, not choose her work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful union handover look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will pass on the street transformer notes and ask a younger member to take them to a branch meeting. The handover matters only if someone keeps checking that residents get power back.

say: **2036 thinking AI** reaches calls before field robots arrive around 2039.
**Outage accountability** should remain clear for residents after I leave repairs.
think: At about **71**, I hope to be off regular line shifts if finances permit.
Our **retirement date** still depends on actual monthly income figures.
do: **Review** retirement statements and set a monthly income target with my partner.
**Keep** street repair shifts while work and health allow.
**Hand** transformer notes to a younger union member at a branch meeting.
feel: **Calm** about personal timing, still engaged with future service to residents.
S4.quote: A power outage still needs a named worker when a resident calls, even if robots lift the transformer.
fieldNote: She links **resident service** to a handover rather than assuming robots solve every outage.
Her own 2039 work status remains **conditional** on affordable retirement figures.

steps.text: Review retirement statements and set monthly income target
Keep street repair shifts while work and health allow
Hand transformer notes to younger union member at branch meeting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because field robots could reduce my line shifts around 2031, before our retirement budget is settled. Written crew plans and a paid route into inspection, if a real post opens, would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who rings the resident after a robot has finished a transformer job. A green light at the power depot is not enough if one resident's flat is still dark. I want the next line crew to own the final check, even after I leave.

headlineQuote: A green light at the power depot is not enough if one resident's flat is still dark.
portrait: **Nora**, 58, repairs city power feeders and transformers after a vocational apprenticeship, with retirement in view.
She uses **AI occasionally** for fault reports and checks addresses against her notebook.
Her **higher pay**, school-cook partner, nine-month savings and nearby utilities give several options.
Fast field robots leave her **anxious** about paid shifts; later scenarios allow union safety work and a careful handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce her line repair shifts around 2031 before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: Written **crew plans** and a paid inspection path, if a real vacancy opens, would help her plan.
